questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)={e}^{\pi x/2}$ about $x=0$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{e}^{\pi x/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot x+(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4})\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\  & =1+\frac{\pi }{2}x+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x}$ about $x=5$ is
questions.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=5,$ we plug $a=5$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(5)+{f}^{′}(5)(x-5)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(5)(x-5)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{x} & ⟹ &  & f(5) & =\frac{6}{5} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(5) & =-\frac{1}{25} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{x}^{-3} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(5) & =\frac{2}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =(\frac{6}{5})+(-\frac{1}{25})\cdot (x-5)+(\frac{2}{125})\cdot \frac{1}{2}(x-5)^{2} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-\frac{1}{25}(x-5)+\frac{1}{125}(x-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Coefficient in a Second-Degree Taylor Polynomial
questions.problem: What is the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}){(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{4})}^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)$ at $x=\frac{1}{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=\frac{1}{4}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(\frac{1}{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{1}{4})(x-\frac{1}{4})+\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{4})}{2}{(x-\frac{1}{4})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{4})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{4})}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{4})=-{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4})=-{\pi }^{2}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=-\frac{\sqrt{2}{\pi }^{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{4})}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{4})}{2} & =\frac{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}{\pi }^{2}}{2})}{2}=-\frac{\sqrt{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
